title: Scale (zoology)
description: Small rigid plate that grows out of an animal's skin
wiki_lead:
In zoology, a scale (Ancient Greek: λεπίς, romanized: lepís; Latin: squāma) is a small rigid plate made out of keratin that grows out of vertebrate animals' skin to provide protection. In lepidopterans (butterflies and moths), scales are plates on the surface of the insect wing, made out of chitin instead of keratin, and provide coloration. Scales are quite common and have evolved multiple times through convergent evolution, with varying structure and function.
Scales are generally classified as part of an organism's integumentary system. There are various types of scales according to the shape and class of an animal.
wiki_excerpt:
In zoology, a scale (Ancient Greek: λεπίς, romanized: lepís; Latin: squāma) is a small rigid plate made out of keratin that grows out of vertebrate animals' skin to provide protection. In lepidopterans (butterflies and moths), scales are plates on the surface of the insect wing, made out of chitin instead of keratin, and provide coloration. Scales are quite common and have evolved multiple times through convergent evolution, with varying structure and function.
Scales are generally classified as part of an organism's integumentary system. There are various types of scales according to the shape and class of an animal.


Fish scales
Fish scales are dermally derived, specifically in the mesoderm. This fact distinguishes them from reptile scales paleontologically.
Genetically, the same genes involved in tooth and hair development in mammals are also involved in scale development.


Cosmoid scales
True cosmoid scales can only be found on the Sarcopterygians. The inner layer of the scale is made of lamellar bone. On top of this lies a layer of spongy or vascular bone and then a layer of dentine-like material called cosmine. The upper surface is keratin. The coelacanth has modified cosmoid scales that lack cosmine and are thinner than true cosmoid scales.


Ganoid scales
Ganoid scales can be found on gars (family Lepisosteidae), bichirs, and reedfishes (family Polypteridae). Ganoid scales are similar to cosmoid scales, but a layer of ganoin lies over the cosmine layer and under the enamel. Ganoin scales are diamond shaped, shiny, and hard.  
Within the ganoin are guanine compounds, iridescent derivatives of guanine found in a DNA molecule. The iridescent property of these chemicals provide the ganoin its shine.


Placoid scales
Placoid scales are found on cartilaginous fish including sharks and stingrays. These scales, also called denticles, are similar in structure to teeth, and have one median spine and two lateral spines. The modern jawed fish ancestors, the jawless ostracoderms and later jawed placoderms, may have had scales with the properties of both placoid and ganoid scales.


Leptoid scales
Leptoid scales are found on higher-order bony fish.  As they grow they add concentric layers. They are arranged so as to overlap in a head-to-tail direction, like roof tiles, allowing a smoother flow of water over the body and therefore reducing drag. They come in two forms:

Cycloid scales have a smooth outer edge, and are most common on fish with soft fin rays, such as salmon and carp.
Ctenoid scales have a toothed outer edge, and are usually found on fish with spiny fin rays, such as bass and crappie.


Reptilian scales

Reptile scale types include cycloid, granular (which appear bumpy), and keeled (which have a center ridge). Scales usually vary in size, the stouter, larger scales cover parts that are often exposed to physical stress (usually the feet, tail and head), while scales are small around the joints for flexibility. Most snakes have extra broad scales on the belly, each scale covering the belly from side to side.
The scales of all reptiles have an epidermal component (what one sees on the surface), but many reptiles, such as crocodilians and turtles, have osteoderms underlying the epidermal scale. Such scales are more properly termed scutes. Snakes, tuataras and many lizards lack osteoderms. All reptilian scales have a dermal papilla underlying the epidermal part, and it is there that the osteoderms, if present, would be formed.
Many reptiles possess large scales not supported by osteoderms known as feature scales. The green iguana possesses large feature scales on the ventral sides of its neck, and dorsal spines not supported by osteoderms. Many extinct non-avian dinosaurs such as Carnotaurus and Brachylophosaurus are known to possess feature scales from skin impressions.

grok_lead: In zoology, a scale is a small, rigid plate that forms part of the integumentary system in various animals, including vertebrates and arthropods, typically derived from epidermal or dermal tissues to provide external protection against predators, abrasion, and environmental stressors. These structures vary widely across animal groups, with dermal scales consisting of bony or tooth-like elements embedded in the dermis and covered by epidermis, as seen in fish, some reptiles, and armadillos, while epidermal scales are keratinized layers of the outer skin, predominant in reptiles, birds, and select mammals. In arthropods, scales often refer to chitinous elements of the exoskeleton or specialized wing coverings. Primarily composed of proteins like keratin (alpha or beta forms) or calcified materials, scales perform essential functions including reducing water loss in terrestrial species, enhancing hydrodynamic efficiency in aquatic locomotion, and facilitating camouflage through pigmentation patterns. In fish, scales are diverse and evolutionarily significant, with four main types: placoid scales (dermal denticles) in cartilaginous fish like sharks, featuring spiny, enamel-covered projections for streamlined swimming and parasite deterrence; ganoid scales in primitive bony fish such as gars, forming hard, enameled plates for robust armor; cycloid scales in many soft-rayed fish like salmon, which are smooth and overlapping for flexibility; and ctenoid scales in spiny-rayed fish like perches, with comb-like edges aiding in maneuverability. These scales often bear growth rings, enabling age determination similar to tree rings, and contribute to overall body flexibility while minimizing drag during movement. Reptilian scales, largely epidermal and overlapping, represent an adaptation to terrestrial life, forming a waterproof barrier via a thick stratum corneum rich in beta-keratins for mechanical strength and alpha-keratins for pliability. In squamates ( lizards and snakes), scales exhibit asymmetry with flexible hinges, allowing body expansion during feeding or shedding, while turtles possess bony scutes over dermal plates for enhanced armor. Functions extend beyond protection to include sensory capabilities, such as mechanoreceptive pits, and thermoregulation through color variation. Birds feature scales primarily on the legs and feet, homologous to reptilian epidermal scales and composed of keratin, providing grip and defense while complementing feathers, often considered modified derivatives of reptilian scalesâfor insulation and flight. Among mammals, scales are rare but notable in pangolins ( Manis spp.), where keratinous, overlapping epidermal scales cover the body, offering flexible yet tough protection against predators and aiding in burrowing behaviors unique to these scaly anteaters, and in armadillos ( Dasypus spp.), where dermal bony plates known as osteoderms form a protective carapace. Overall, scales exemplify convergent evolution in animal integuments, balancing protection with mobility across diverse habitats.
